At one nest, the helper was one of the previous year's offspring of the adult female and a different male (Brackbill 1970b). Does not occur. Occasional observations of males feeding begging incubating females that are not their mates. Routine feeding of fledglings by unrelated adults, especially males. Behavior is particularly common at feeders when juveniles beg from adults. Older broods commonly join and 10-15 juveniles beg for food from a single adult male. In w. Montana, close association of two males and a female in some nests (Cole 2002), although only one male fathers and feeds nestlings in such nests.

At 25 Vermont nests observed by videography, one female fed at each nest, with two provisioning males most common (60%), followed by nests with one provisioning male (20%), nests with three males (16%), and nests with four males (4%; VCE). Four males documented to feed at >1 nest within single breeding season, and three males fed two broods simultaneously (nests 186–443 m apart). One male simultaneously provisioned at two nests 443 m apart, shared feeding of nestlings at first nest, was sole male feeder at second nest. First nest fledged 3 d after second nest hatched; male then left care of fledglings to the other male and fed second brood at nearly twice the rate as he had fed young at first nest. Individual female, total male, and total adult provisioning rates did not differ between nests with single and multiple male feeders. The number of male feeders was negatively correlated to prey abundance on female home ranges, suggesting that females might balance the cost of low prey abundance by copulating with multiple males and attracting male feeders (Strong et al. 2004). Overall, females fed nestlings at more than twice the rate of males (Goetz et al 2003). Male feeding rates increased with nestling age until day 7–8 and then decreased until fledging. Some males did not feed at nests in which they sired young, and some males fed at nests in which they sired no young (Goetz et al. 2003). Multiple male feeders also reported at nests in Quebec (Y. Aubry) and New Brunswick (Askanas 2012). In highlands of New Brunswick, 78% of nests had two or more male feeders (Askanas 2012). At five nests females provided 57±15% of the feeds at a nest, individual males 21±9%. In Quebec three males attended two different nests in one breeding season (Y. Aubry unpubl.). I

Females only incubate and brood the young, but both males and females bring food to the nestlings. Group members help during nesting. Helpers contribute with nest defense and feeding nestlings; helpers start feeding nestlings on day 5 after hatching and, on average, they make 4.5% (18 of the 397) of the total feeding trips (Willis 1961).

Nests often attract the attention of extra adults that associate with a pair for up to an entire breeding season; these extra birds are sometimes tolerated and occasionally lead to polygyny (217). In New York, extra birds were predominantly males (219, 325), whereas in Washington, extra birds were yearling females (217). Extra adults contribute relatively little to feeding young, but they are known to mob predators and assist in nest-building, incubation, and brooding young (219, 325, 217). Extra adults may be using nest attendance as a breeding strategy either to replace one pair member should something happen to it (217) or to commit sexually selected infanticide (219, 325), providing an opportunity for males to take over the breeding female (see Behavior: Sexual Behavior). Nests that are attended by helpers often are ones occupied by older females (325), consistent with the interpretation that male attendants are trying to secure high-quality females as mates.

Although ca. 20% of Canada Jay pairs studied in Quebec and Ontario have an associated nonbreeder on their territories at the onset of breeding and ca. 65% of these are the pair's own offspring from the previous breeding season, the nonbreeders do not feed the current year's nestlings and the breeders energetically drive them away if they approach the nest. Starting immediately after the nestlings fledge, however, adults relax this vigilance and on intensively observed territories in Ontario and Quebec some non-breeders have accounted for over 30% of all observed feedings of the young (189, 190). Proposed explanation for this pattern holds that, compared to other jays, Canada Jays are particularly vulnerable to nest predators because they have poorer defensive abilities (being smaller and generally having only one extra group member, if any). In such a species, suppression of allofeeding, along with a smaller than expected clutch size and a very low provisioning rate by the adults (achieved by bringing largest possible loads at the consequently minimum possible frequency), may reduce predator-attracting visits to the nest and thus contribute to higher breeding success (166, 191). Polygynandrous mating system, 2–5 males share large overlapping ranges of 2–5 females, group ranges (9–38 ha) more or less exclusive; males compete to mate with fertile females, females compete to attract males; solicitation display by female, which has high copulation rate (up to 1000 per clutch), usually involving several males. Five breeding groups studied in a Swiss alpine region each consisted of 1–4 females with exclusive territories, and 3–5 males which co-operated in defending group territory; within group, linear dominance relationship usually well established among alpha, beta and subordinate males, both frequent copulation and mate-guarding strategies being used, and females advertised their fertility, solicited most of copulations and mated many times with several males (c. 350 matings during short fertile period of ten days), while intensity of mate-guarding and copulation frequency were highest on day preceding and throughout laying period; in this polygynandrous system, females of studied population lacked full male help but might have benefited from greater genetic variation of their offspring, while males varied widely in lifetime reproductive success, higher-ranking males raising their fitness to above average (4). Nest, built by female, a cup made from grass, moss and plant stems, lined with hair and feathers, sited in rock crevice or beneath rock or grass tussock on cliff or shallower slope. Cooperative breeding is apparently rare (< 0.1%), but is likely to be under-reported because it requires detailed observation. Fledglings have been observed helping build nests (Tarwater 2006). This appears to be more beneficial for offspring in terms of learning rather than helping parents. The fledglings collected nest material and in some cases they put the nesting material on the nest (but did not actually weave the material into the nest) and in other cases they dropped the nesting material while trying to fly with it. Older fledglings, which have developed the ability to sing, will help defend the natal territory with their parents (Tarwater 2006).

Extremely rare if not absent in most temperate populations. One report from California of a juvenile from a first brood helping its father (and possibly mother; she was unmarked) feed young of a second brood in the same season (275. Second report from Kansas of a juvenile of unknown origin feeding young and removing a fecal sac from a nest at least one time (Timson and Farley 2003). Helpers-at-the-nest also reported in Costa Rica, but not in all nests and such behavior was apparently rare (Skutch 1940, 176, Skutch 1983, Winnett-Murray 1986). Skutch (1983) speculated helping was more likely when young from a previous brood sleep with the mother in the nest while she incubates in a subsequent breeding attempt. In one case in Costa Rica, an individual known not to be the offspring of a resident parents' previous brood attempted to feed young; parents repeatedly attacked that individual (Winnett-Murray 1986: 23).

Does not occur (17, MTM). Trios of adults occasionally form, but are rarely stable; a trio in New York remained together from early in nestling period to > 1 mo after young had fledged (MTM). The fate of the third bird in next year was determined in 2 of 3 cases in which the third bird was banded and sex determined. In one case, a female returned to breed on territory where she was seen in previous year (former male and female occupants of territory failed to return). In the other case, a male established residence on adjacent territory in following year. Third birds in trios probably represent birds prospecting for a breeding site in the next year.
